claim: Null mutations in the Dp427 isoform of the dystrophin gene result in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD).
source: Null mutations in the Dp427 isoform of the dystrophin gene result Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) (Hoffman et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoffman et al., 1987

claim: DMD is an inheritable X-linked disease that affects primarily adolescent males causing progressive skeletal muscle deterioration.
source: This inheritable X-linked disease affects primarily adolescent males causing progressive skeletal muscle deterioration, with negative effects in the central nervous system (Anderson et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2002

claim: Muscular dystrophies are characterized by cardiac muscle involvement.
source: Muscular dystrophies are also characterized by cardiac muscle involvement (Corrado et al., 2002), which usually starts with an abnormal ECG (Finsterer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corrado et al., 2002 and Finsterer et al., 2018

claim: Most patients with DMD will develop cardiomyopathy by 20 years of age.
source: Eventually, most patients with DMD will develop cardiomyopathy by 20 years of age (Shirokova and Niggli, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shirokova and Niggli, 2013

claim: Many DMD patients will be at a high risk for arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death (SCD).
source: Many will be at a high risk for arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death (SCD), which contributes considerably to the morbidity and mortality of the disease (Yilmaz and Sechtem, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yilmaz and Sechtem, 2012

claim: Diagnosis and prevention of arrhythmia are challenging in DMD patients.
source: However, diagnosis and prevention of arrhythmia are challenging in DMD patients (Yilmaz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yilmaz et al., 2009

claim: The mechanisms responsible for arrhythmias and SCD in patients with DMD cardiomyopathy are poorly understood.
source: The mechanisms responsible for arrhythmias and SCD in patients with DMD cardiomyopathy are poorly understood.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap in the field

claim: The dystrophin-associated protein complex (DAPC) is involved in mechanoprotection of the plasma membrane.
source: The dystrophin-associated protein complex (DAPC) is involved in mechanoprotection of the plasma membrane (Petrof et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Petrof et al., 1993

claim: The DAPC acts as a putative cellular signaling complex that forms a scaffold for numerous signaling and membrane ion channel proteins.
source: The DAPC acts also as a putative cellular signaling complex that forms a scaffold for numerous signaling and membrane ion channel proteins (Constantin, 2014; Gavillet et al., 2006; Milstein et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Constantin, 2014; Gavillet et al., 2006; Milstein et al., 2012

claim: The absence of dystrophin in DMD has the potential to alter trafficking, localization, and function of DAPC-associated proteins in skeletal and cardiac muscle.
source: The absence of dystrophin in DMD has the potential to alter trafficking, localization, and function of DAPC-associated proteins in skeletal and cardiac muscle (Lohan et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lohan et al., 2005

claim: The expression and function of ion channels are defective in ventricular cardiomyocytes of the mdx mouse model.
source: For example, the expression and function of ion channels are defective in ventricular cardiomyocytes of the mdx mouse model (Gavillet et al., 2006; Koenig et al., 2014; Rubi et al., 2017; Koenig et al., 2011; Albesa et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gavillet et al., 2006; Koenig et al., 2014; Rubi et al., 2017; Koenig et al., 2011; Albesa et al., 2011

claim: The absence of dystrophin in young mdx mice affects the function of NaV1.5, leading to cardiac conduction defects.
source: The absence of dystrophin in young mdx mice affects the function of NaV1.5, leading to cardiac conduction defects (Gavillet et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gavillet et al., 2006

claim: Inward rectifier potassium current IK1 is reduced in the mdx mouse.
source: Inward rectifier potassium current IK1 is reduced in the mdx mouse (Rubi et al., 2017) but the consequences of the disruption have not been identified.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rubi et al., 2017

claim: NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 control cardiac excitability by mutually modulating each other's surface expression.
source: Results from our laboratory and others strongly suggest that NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 control cardiac excitability by mutually modulating each other's surface expression (Milstein et al., 2012; Albesa et al., 2011; Petitprez et al., 2011; Leonoudakis et al., 2004; Matamoros et al., 2016; Ponce-Balbuena et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Milstein et al., 2012; Albesa et al., 2011; Petitprez et al., 2011; Leonoudakis et al., 2004; Matamoros et al., 2016; Ponce-Balbuena et al., 2018

claim: At the lateral membrane, NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 channels form macromolecular complexes ('channelosomes') that include α1-syntrophin.
source: At the lateral membrane, NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 channels form macromolecular complexes ('channelosomes') (Pérez-Hernández et al., 2018) that include α1-syntrophin, which is a part of the DAPC (Gavillet et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pérez-Hernández et al., 2018 and Gavillet et al., 2006

claim: iPSC-CMs from patients with DMD cardiomyopathy have a dysfunction of the NaV1.5–Kir2.1 channelosome.
source: We demonstrate here that patient-specific iPSC-CMs recapitulated consistently the hallmark electrophysiologic features of cardiomyopathic DMD patients (Finsterer and Stöllberger, 2003), In fact, mature iPSC-CMs from two hemizygous male DMD patients lacking the Dp427 isoform and a female patient heterozygous for a 5-exon deletion (Δ8–12) in the dystrophin gene have significantly reduced INa and IK1 densities, dV/dtmax and conduction velocities, as well as focal and reentrant arrhythmias.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced INa and IK1 densities in DMD iPSC-CMs

claim: Two DMD patients had abnormal ECGs with frequent runs of ventricular tachycardia.
source: Two patients had abnormal ECGs with frequent runs of ventricular tachycardia.
evidence: Clinical observation reported in the abstract

claim: iPSC-CMs from all DMD patients showed abnormal action potential profiles.
source: iPSC-CMs from all DMD patients showed abnormal action potential profiles, slowed conduction velocities, and reduced sodium (INa) and inward rectifier potassium (IK1) currents.
evidence: Experimental findings from patch-clamp recordings

claim: iPSC-CMs from all DMD patients showed slowed conduction velocities.
source: iPSC-CMs from all DMD patients showed abnormal action potential profiles, slowed conduction velocities, and reduced sodium (INa) and inward rectifier potassium (IK1) currents.
evidence: Experimental findings from optical mapping experiments

claim: iPSC-CMs from all DMD patients showed reduced sodium (INa) currents.
source: iPSC-CMs from all DMD patients showed abnormal action potential profiles, slowed conduction velocities, and reduced sodium (INa) and inward rectifier potassium (IK1) currents.
evidence: Experimental findings from patch-clamp recordings

claim: iPSC-CMs from all DMD patients showed reduced inward rectifier potassium (IK1) currents.
source: iPSC-CMs from all DMD patients showed abnormal action potential profiles, slowed conduction velocities, and reduced sodium (INa) and inward rectifier potassium (IK1) currents.
evidence: Experimental findings from patch-clamp recordings

claim: Membrane NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 protein levels were reduced in hemizygous DMD iPSC-CMs.
source: Membrane NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 protein levels were reduced in hemizygous DMD iPSC-CMs but not in heterozygous iPSC-CMs.
evidence: Experimental findings from biotinylation assays

claim: Membrane NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 protein levels were not reduced in heterozygous iPSC-CMs.
source: Membrane NaV1.5 and Kir2.1 protein levels were reduced in hemizygous DMD iPSC-CMs but not in heterozygous iPSC-CMs.
evidence: Experimental findings from biotinylation assays

claim: Transfecting α1-syntrophin in hemizygous iPSC-CMs from one patient restored channelosome function.
source: Remarkably, transfecting just one component of the dystrophin protein complex (α1-syntrophin) in hemizygous iPSC-CMs from one patient restored channelosome function, INa and IK1 densities, and action potential profile in single cells.
evidence: Experimental findings from SNTA1 transfection experiments

claim: Transfecting α1-syntrophin in hemizygous iPSC-CMs from one patient restored INa and IK1 densities.
source: Remarkably, transfecting just one component of the dystrophin protein complex (α1-syntrophin) in hemizygous iPSC-CMs from one patient restored channelosome function, INa and IK1 densities, and action potential profile in single cells.
evidence: Experimental findings from patch-clamp recordings after SNTA1 transfection

claim: Transfecting α1-syntrophin in hemizygous iPSC-CMs from one patient restored action potential profile in single cells.
source: Remarkably, transfecting just one component of the dystrophin protein complex (α1-syntrophin) in hemizygous iPSC-CMs from one patient restored channelosome function, INa and IK1 densities, and action potential profile in single cells.
evidence: Experimental findings from patch-clamp recordings after SNTA1 transfection

claim: α1-syntrophin expression restored impulse conduction in hiPSC-CM monolayers.
source: In addition, α1-syntrophin expression restored impulse conduction and contractility and prevented reentrant arrhythmias in hiPSC-CM monolayers.
evidence: Experimental findings from optical mapping experiments after SNTA1 transfection

claim: α1-syntrophin expression restored contractility in hiPSC-CM monolayers.
source: In addition, α1-syntrophin expression restored impulse conduction and contractility and prevented reentrant arrhythmias in hiPSC-CM monolayers.
evidence: Experimental findings from contractility assays after SNTA1 transfection

claim: α1-syntrophin expression prevented reentrant arrhythmias in hiPSC-CM monolayers.
source: In addition, α1-syntrophin expression restored impulse conduction and contractility and prevented reentrant arrhythmias in hiPSC-CM monolayers.
evidence: Experimental findings from optical mapping experiments after SNTA1 transfection

claim: Reduced excitability underlies the arrhythmogenic mechanism in DMD patients.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that reduced excitability underlies the arrhythmogenic mechanism in DMD patients.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing reduced INa, IK1, and conduction velocity

claim: The hemizygous male (Male 1) harbored a nonsense point mutation in the dystrophin gene (exon 41).
source: The hemizygous male (Male 1) harboring a nonsense point mutation in the dystrophin gene (exon 41) experienced DMD from early childhood, being diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy at age 17.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: Male 1 experienced DMD from early childhood and was diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy at age 17.
source: The hemizygous male (Male 1) harboring a nonsense point mutation in the dystrophin gene (exon 41) experienced DMD from early childhood, being diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy at age 17.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: Male 1 was hospitalized in respiratory and heart failure (LVEF = 15%) at age 25, requiring tracheostomy and prolonged ventilation.
source: Eight years later he was hospitalized in respiratory and heart failure (LVEF = 15%), requiring tracheostomy and prolonged ventilation.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: An ECG of Male 1 exhibited sinus rhythm with a narrow QRS and QR pattern in L1, AVL, and QS leads V2–3.
source: An ECG exhibited sinus rhythm with a narrow QRS and QR pattern in L1, AVL, and QS leads V2–3 (Figure 1a).
evidence: Clinical ECG data shown in Figure 1a

claim: A routine Holter-ECG of Male 1 at age 33 showed frequent premature ventricular complexes and episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia at rates of up to 200/min.
source: A routine Holter-ECG obtained 3 years later showed frequent premature ventricular complexes and episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia at rates of up to 200/min.
evidence: Clinical Holter-ECG data from patient records

claim: An ICD was implanted in Male 1, which discharged appropriately 2 years later for repeated episodes of ventricular flutter deteriorating into ventricular fibrillation.
source: An ICD was implanted, which discharged appropriately 2 years later for repeated episodes of ventricular flutter deteriorating into ventricular fibrillation (Figure 1b).
evidence: Clinical ICD data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Male 1 expired of heart failure at age 38.
source: Three years later, the patient expired of heart failure at age 38.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: The female patient was heterozygous for a deletion of five exons (Δ8–12) in the dystrophin gene.
source: The female patient, heterozygous for a deletion of five exons (Δ8–12) in the dystrophin gene, presented proximal muscle weakness with creatine kinase elevation at age 42.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: The female patient presented proximal muscle weakness with creatine kinase elevation at age 42.
source: The female patient, heterozygous for a deletion of five exons (Δ8–12) in the dystrophin gene, presented proximal muscle weakness with creatine kinase elevation at age 42.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: At presentation, the female patient exhibited biventricular dysfunction with left ventricular dimension of 65 mm, LVEF of 30% and moderate-to-severe mitral insufficiency.
source: At presentation, she exhibited biventricular dysfunction with left ventricular dimension of 65 mm, LVEF of 30% and moderate-to-severe mitral insufficiency.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: At age 49, the female patient developed severe biventricular dysfunction with LVEF = 20% and severe tricuspid regurgitation.
source: At age 49, she developed severe biventricular dysfunction with LVEF = 20% and severe tricuspid regurgitation.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: The female patient was in NYHA IV with a VO2 max of 6 ml/kg/min, indicating a severely reduced aerobic capacity.
source: She was in NYHA IV, and the cardiorespiratory exercise test showed a VO2 max of 6 ml/kg/min, indicating a severely reduced aerobic capacity.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: An ECG of the female patient obtained at age 50 revealed severe QRS widening and QT prolongation.
source: An ECG obtained at age 50 revealed severe QRS widening and QT prolongation (Figure 1c).
evidence: Clinical ECG data shown in Figure 1c

claim: At age 51, the female patient developed paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and recurrent episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia.
source: A year later, she developed paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and recurrent episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (Figure 1d).
evidence: Clinical data shown in Figure 1d

claim: The female patient required AV nodal ablation and CRTD pacemaker-defibrillator implantation.
source: AV nodal ablation and CRTD pacemaker-defibrillator implantation were required.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: The female patient died at 51 in end-stage heart failure associated with renal insufficiency.
source: The patient died at 51 in end-stage heart failure associated with renal insufficiency.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: Male 2 was a 13-year-old male carrying a 6-exon dystrophin deletion (Δ45–50).
source: The additional DMD patient (Male 2) was a 13-year-old male carrying a 6-exon dystrophin deletion (Δ45–50).
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: Male 2 was nonambulatory (used a motorized wheelchair) but respirator free at the time of the skin biopsy.
source: The patient was nonambulatory (used a motorized wheelchair) but respirator free at the time of the skin biopsy.
evidence: Clinical data from patient records

claim: Male 2 did not have significant cardiomyopathy at the time of collection.
source: He did not have significant cardiomyopathy at the time of collection, which was not surprising given his young age and the typical presentation of DMD cardiomyopathy as later onset (de Souza et al., 2020; Szabo et al., 2021).
evidence: Clinical data from patient records with citations to de Souza et al., 2020; Szabo et al., 2021

claim: iPSC-CMs from hemizygous males were deficient in the full-length adult DP427 dystrophin isoform.
source: Compared to Control-1 iPSC-CMs and to left ventricle samples from a patient with Becker dystrophy, iPSC-CMs from hemizygous males were deficient in the full-length adult DP427 dystrophin isoform (Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 2a,b

claim: The iPSC line named Male 2 shows a deletion of exons 45–50.
source: The iPSC line named Male 2 shows a deletion of exons 45–50, while the other dystrophic cell line (Male 1) presents a nonsense point mutation (R1967X) in exon 41 of the dystrophin gene constituting a premature stop codon.
evidence: Genetic characterization of the cell line

claim: Male 1 presents a nonsense point mutation (R1967X) in exon 41 of the dystrophin gene constituting a premature stop codon.
source: The iPSC line named Male 2 shows a deletion of exons 45–50, while the other dystrophic cell line (Male 1) presents a nonsense point mutation (R1967X) in exon 41 of the dystrophin gene constituting a premature stop codon.
evidence: Genetic characterization of the cell line

claim: The cell line generated from the 50-year-old DMD heterozygous female carried a deletion of exons 8–12.
source: The cell line generated from the 50-year-old DMD heterozygous female carried a deletion of exons 8–12.
evidence: Genetic characterization of the cell line

claim: iPSC-CMs from the heterozygous female showed expression of dystrophin protein like the control.
source: Notably, her iPSC-CMs showed expression of dystrophin protein like the control.
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 2a,b

claim: Dystrophin was absent in DMD iPSC-CMs compared to control iPSC-CMs.
source: Dystrophin was absent in DMD iPSC-CMs (p = 0.0001) compared to control iPSC-CMs.
evidence: Western blot quantification shown in Figure 2b with statistical significance

claim: Heterozygous female cells exhibited nearly normal dystrophin expression.
source: Heterozygous female cells exhibited nearly normal dystrophin expression (p = 0.5864).
evidence: Western blot quantification shown in Figure 2b with statistical significance

claim: DMD cells did not express dystrophin compared to control.
source: DMD cells did not express dystrophin compared to control.
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Heterozygous female iPSC-CMs showed variable expression of dystrophin.
source: Heterozygous female iPSC-CMs showed variable expression of dystrophin.
evidence: Immunostaining data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Cell shape is critical for cardiomyocyte electrical, mechanical, and contractile function.
source: Cell shape is critical for cardiomyocyte electrical, mechanical, and contractile function (Kuo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuo et al., 2012

claim: Adopting the typical cylindrical morphology helps improve contractility, which promotes electrophysiological phenotype maturation.
source: Adopting the typical cylindrical morphology helps improve contractility, which promotes electrophysiological phenotype maturation (Ribeiro et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ribeiro et al., 2015

claim: When cultured on a nonmicropatterned smooth surface, DMD iPSC-CMs are flat shaped and have a frail membrane making them a challenge for patch-clamp experiments.
source: When cultured on a nonmicropatterned smooth surface, DMD iPSC-CMs are flat shaped and have a frail membrane making them a challenge for patch-clamp experiments (Figure 2c, left).
evidence: Observation from experimental work shown in Figure 2c

claim: Micropatterning produces large numbers of thick cylindrical-shaped, binucleated cardiomyocytes with well-organized sarcomeres.
source: The approach produces large numbers of thick cylindrical-shaped, binucleated cardiomyocytes with well-organized sarcomeres (Figure 2d), which are two important signs of maturation.
evidence: Observation from experimental work shown in Figure 2d

claim: Micropatterned iPSC-CMs are easier to patch.
source: Micropatterned iPSC-CMs are easier to patch.
evidence: Observation from experimental work

claim: Micropatterned iPSC-CMs are electrically excitable and their electrical phenotype approaches the adult human cardiomyocyte, with maximum diastolic potentials (MDP) of −70 to −80 mV, and APDs of 200–300 ms.
source: They are electrically excitable and their electrical phenotype approaches the adult human cardiomyocyte, with maximum diastolic potentials (MDP) of −70 to −80 mV, and APDs of 200–300 ms (see below; Taggart et al., 1996; Grandi et al., 2011).
evidence: Observation from experimental work with citations to Taggart et al., 1996; Grandi et al., 2011

claim: DMD patients may experience cardiac complications and often exhibit electrical conduction abnormalities and life-threatening arrhythmias.
source: Clinically, DMD patients may experience cardiac complications and often exhibit electrical conduction abnormalities and life-threatening arrhythmias (see Figure 1; Fayssoil et al., 2010; Finsterer and Stöllberger, 2003)
evidence: Clinical observations with citations to Fayssoil et al., 2010; Finsterer and Stöllberger, 2003

claim: At the cellular level, electrical conduction abnormalities and life-threatening arrhythmias are often the result of reduced excitability.
source: At the cellular level, such alterations are often the result of reduced excitability.
evidence: Inference from established knowledge about cardiac electrophysiology

claim: Controls 1 and 2 were very similar to each other, both exhibiting well-polarized MDPs, dV/dtmax larger than 40 V/s and amplitudes larger than 100 mV.
source: Statistical analysis demonstrated that Controls 1 and 2 were very similar to each other, both exhibiting well-polarized MDPs, dV/dtmax larger than 40 V/s and amplitudes larger than 100 mV.
evidence: Statistical analysis of patch-clamp data

claim: Controls 1 and 2 both differed significantly from all three DMD groups, particularly in terms of dV/dtmax.
source: However, they both differed significantly from all three DMD groups (Figure 3—source data 1; and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-f), particularly in terms of dV/dtmax.
evidence: Statistical analysis of patch-clamp data shown in Figure 3

claim: iPSC-CMs from both DMD male and female patients revealed abnormal AP profiles compared to both controls.
source: iPSC-CMs from both DMD male and female patients revealed abnormal AP profiles compared to both controls.
evidence: Patch-clamp data analysis

claim: Overshoot and amplitude were lower in the Male 2 cells compared to the controls.
source: For example, overshoot and amplitude were lower in the Male 2 cells compared to the controls.
evidence: Patch-clamp data shown in Figure 3c,d

claim: Female DMD cells showed a more depolarized MDP than control iPSC-CMs.
source: In addition, female DMD cells showed a more depolarized MDP than control iPSC-CMs (Figure 3e).
evidence: Patch-clamp data shown in Figure 3e

claim: No significant differences existed in APD90 values among control and DMD iPSC-CMs.
source: Finally, no significant differences existed in APD90 values and similar action potential parameter changes were obtained at 2 Hz (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Patch-clamp data analysis

claim: CV in dystrophin-deficient iPSC-CM monolayers was 50% slower than control monolayers paced at 1 Hz.
source: CV in dystrophin-deficient iPSC-CM monolayers was 50% slower than control monolayers paced at 1 Hz (27 ± 2 and 29 ± 4 cm/s in hemizygous Males 1 and 2 cells, respectively, versus 56 ± 3 cm/s in control cells, Figure 4b, c).
evidence: Optical mapping data shown in Figure 4b,c

claim: CV of Control 2 monolayers was 42 ± 5 cm/s.
source: CV of Control 2 monolayers was 42 ± 5 cm/s (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Optical mapping data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: CV in the heterozygous female monolayers was 18 ± 3 cm/s.
source: Remarkably, CV in the heterozygous female monolayers was even slower (18 ± 3 cm/s).
evidence: Optical mapping data

claim: In all three DMD groups, the CV restitution curve displayed slightly slower velocities at higher frequencies.
source: In all three groups, the CV restitution curve displayed slightly slower velocities at higher frequencies (Figure 4d).
evidence: Optical mapping data shown in Figure 4d

claim: In the female monolayer, slower and more heterogeneous patterns of electrical wave propagation were accompanied by focal discharges in the form of trigeminy.
source: Most important, in the female monolayer (Figure 4e), slower and more heterogeneous patterns of electrical wave propagation were accompanied by focal discharges in the form of trigeminy (Figure 4e, left), which often triggered unidirectional block and reentry (Figure 4e, right).
evidence: Optical mapping data shown in Figure 4e

claim: Focal discharges in the female monolayer often triggered unidirectional block and reentry.
source: Most important, in the female monolayer (Figure 4e), slower and more heterogeneous patterns of electrical wave propagation were accompanied by focal discharges in the form of trigeminy (Figure 4e, left), which often triggered unidirectional block and reentry (Figure 4e, right).
evidence: Optical mapping data shown in Figure 4e

claim: The reduced CV in all three iPSC-CMs from affected individuals occurred in the absence of measurable changes in connexin43 (Cx43) protein.
source: In all three iPSC-CMs from affected individuals, the reduced CV occurred in the absence of measurable changes in connexin43 (Cx43) protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: No significant differences in Cx43 expression were detected among control, heterozygous, and hemizygous iPSC-CMs in monolayer experiments.
source: We did not detect any significant differences in Cx43 expression among control, heterozygous, and hemizygous iPSC-CMs in these monolayer experiments.
evidence: Western blot data analysis

claim: Sodium channels determine the upstroke velocity of the cardiac action potential and consequently play a key role in the conduction of the cardiac electrical impulse.
source: Sodium channels determine the upstroke velocity of the cardiac action potential and consequently play a key role in the conduction of the cardiac electrical impulse (Abriel, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abriel, 2007

claim: The peak inward INa density in hemizygous iPSC-CMs was significantly decreased compared to both Control 1 and Control 2 iPSC-CMs.
source: In Figure 5a,b, Figure 5—source data 1, the peak inward INa density in hemizygous iPSC-CMs was significantly decreased (−14 ± 1 pA/pF for Male 1 cells and −15 ± 1 pA/pF for Male 2 cells) compared to both Control 1 (−27 ± 3 pA/pF) and Control 2 iPSC-CMs (−38 ± 1 pA/pF; Figure 5—figure supplement 1g, Supplementary files 4 and 5).
evidence: Patch-clamp data shown in Figure 5a,b

claim: The INa density in heterozygous female cells was dramatically reduced.
source: Importantly, the INa density in heterozygous female cells was also dramatically reduced (−11 ± 1 pA/pF).
evidence: Patch-clamp data

claim: Statistical comparisons in terms of biophysical properties of INa (half maximal activation, slope factor, reversal potential) showed no differences among any of the groups.
source: Altogether, except for peak sodium current density, statistical comparisons in terms of biophysical properties of INa (half maximal activation, slope factor, reversal potential) for DMD versus Control 1 (Supplementary file 4), DMD versus Control 2 (Supplementary file 5), and Control 1 versus Control 2 (Supplementary file 6) showed no differences among any of the groups.
evidence: Statistical analysis of patch-clamp data

claim: Cell capacitance in all the patient-specific cells was similar to control, indicating that cell size was similar in all groups.
source: Also, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, cell capacitance in all the patient-specific cells was similar to control, indicating that cell size was similar in all groups.
evidence: Patch-clamp data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: ICa,L density is increased in cardiomyocytes from adult mdx mice.
source: For instance, the L-type calcium current (ICa,L) is increased in cardiomyocytes from adult mdx mice (Koenig et al., 2014; Viola et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koenig et al., 2014; Viola et al., 2013

claim: ICa,L density is increased in iPSC-CMs from DMD patients according to previous studies.
source: In addition, as previously suggested, ICa,L density is increased in iPSC-CMs from DMD patients (Yotsukura et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yotsukura et al., 1992

claim: Under the experimental conditions of this study, ICa,L was unaltered in hemizygous and heterozygous DMD iPSC-CMs.
source: However, under our experimental conditions, ICa,L was unaltered in hemizygous and heterozygous DMD iPSC-CMs (Supplementary files 4 and 6; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Patch-clamp data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: The DAPC regulates Kir2.1 inward rectifying potassium channels in mdx cardiomyocytes.
source: Apart from the well-described regulation of NaV1.5 channels by the DAPC (Gavillet et al., 2006; Petitprez et al., 2011), there is evidence that this protein complex also regulates Kir2.1 inward rectifying potassium channels in mdx cardiomyocytes (Rubi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gavillet et al., 2006; Petitprez et al., 2011; Rubi et al., 2017

claim: A pool of NaV1.5 channels colocalizes with Kir2.1 forming protein complexes with scaffolding proteins at the cardiomyocyte lateral membrane and intercalated disc.
source: Moreover, a pool of NaV1.5 channels colocalizes with Kir2.1 forming protein complexes with scaffolding proteins at the cardiomyocyte lateral membrane and intercalated disc, where they modulate each other's surface expression (Milstein et al., 2012; Matamoros et al., 2016; Ponce-Balbuena et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Milstein et al., 2012; Matamoros et al., 2016; Ponce-Balbuena et al., 2018

claim: IK1 density measured at −120 mV was significantly reduced in Male 1 and Male 2 iPSC-CMs compared to Control 1.
source: In Figure 5c, d, Figure 5—source data 1, IK1 density measured at −120 mV was significantly reduced in Male 1 (−1 ± 0.3 pA/pF) and Male 2 (−1.2 ± 0.3 pA/pF) iPSC-CMs compared to Control 1 (−3.2 ± 0.5 pA/pF).
evidence: Patch-clamp data shown in Figure 5c,d

claim: IK1 density of Control 2 cells was −2.6 ± 0.6 pA/pF.
source: IK1 density of Control 2 cells was −2.6 ± 0.6 pA/pF.
evidence: Patch-clamp data

claim: Changes in IK1 were highly variable in heterozygous cells, and the difference with control was not significant.
source: Changes in IK1 were highly variable in heterozygous cells, and the difference with control was not significant, likely due to the variability of expression of dystrophin (Figure 2e) and other proteins forming the complex.
evidence: Patch-clamp data analysis with inference about the cause

claim: When one of the DAPC components is genetically absent, other proteins of the complex are likewise downregulated, leading to a dysfunction of the complex.
source: Previous reports have shown that when one of the DAPC components is genetically absent, other proteins of the complex are likewise downregulated, leading to a dysfunction of the complex (Araishi et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Araishi et al., 1999

claim: Both hemizygous DMD iPSC-CMs showed increased SCN5A expression.
source: Consistent with what has been described for mdx mice (Gavillet et al., 2006), both hemizygous DMD iPSC-CMs showed increased SCN5A expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 3a, top), also like human cardiac tissue from a Becker MD (BMD) individual (Figure 5—figure supplement 3a, bottom).
